newsitem.title: UK: Bruised convertible bond buyers become selective.
newsitem.headline: Bruised convertible bond buyers become selective.

text.p: Eastern European and Russian companies may speed up plans for convertible bond issues to tap into the market's improved sentiment following Russian oil giant LUKoil's successful deal last week, bankers said on Thursday.

But investors, whose confidence in the emerging convertible bond sector was bruised by a disastrous deal from Poland's Stalexport SA in March, would remain wary about which companies to buy into, they said.
"Some may accelerate issuance, I'm sure of that, but investors have learned from Stalexport to be selective. Those issues that are not the highest of quality will struggle," said one specialist.
"Stalexport investors immediately lost five percent. A lot of them won't even take a phone call about Polish convertibles," he added.
Stalexport's $50 million convertible bond issue was 79 percent oversubscribed, but the bonds subsequently traded down to 95 from par, crushing market sentiment.
Yet LUKoil last week sold $200 million five-year convertible bonds. The deal was five times oversubscribed, and the bonds have remained buoyant.
There remains a long list of Russian, Polish and Hungarian companies that plan to raise month with convertibles.
Convertible bonds provide a low-risk alternative to gain exposure in booming equity markets. They pay a relatively low coupon, but give investors the option to swap the bond for shares.
Demand for convertible bonds is still strong, reflecting investors' cautionary stance about financial markets because of recent volatility, said Richard Roberts, assistant director of WestMerchant.
"The jury is still out on whether (convertibles from emerging markets) will develop into a full blown sector, but I think it will," Roberts added.
Many specialists said they were reserving judgement until a few more deals were completed.

"LUKoil was one convertible bond transaction that traded well, but it's not a reason to stumble over yourself to get into the market," said the director of convertible research at one major investment bank.

Russian oil producer Sidanko is planning a convertible bond issue, which would be the second Russian convertible issue, and specialists say it has a good chance of being well received since the company is fairly well known and has a relatively broad pre-existing equity base.
"Our best advice is that a company should expand its equity base before trying to launch convertibles," said a specialist with a major U.S. investment bank.
He said that part of the reason LUKoil's convertible debut was successful was because the company had an equity base as well as listed global depositary receipts.
Unified Energy System of Russia faces more of a challenge unless the deal is well marketed, specialists said.
Polish convertible issues in the pipeline are due from Bank Przemyslowo-Handlowy SA and Elektrim, both of which have a good chance of attracting investors' interest, specialists said.
"They still have to get the pricing and the structure right," a specialist said.
Issues planned by Poland's Bank Komunalny SA and by Wolczanka could meet resistance unless they are very attractively priced, they said.
Polish convertible issues are a bit less popular with investors because Polish laws require a series of approvals to convert bonds into shares, they added.
Another specialist said he expected at least one of Hungary's leading oil firms to issue convertible bonds before the end of this year.

"The equity markets have performed well in Russia, eastern Europe, and there's a lot of interest. It's the most favoured emerging markets area. The prospects are good," said Katalin Tischhauser, head of convertibles research at SBC Warburg.
"The demand is certainly there. The environment for the convertibles market is so healthy and so strong. It would make sense to for (issuers) to move quickly," she added.
